income_by_occupation.stated: Annual wage = daily wage x 260 days (five days a week, 52 weeks).
income_by_occupation.note: An assumption, not an observed count of days worked. The same authors (2019) argue day-wage incomes overstate medieval earnings because labourers worked fewer days; see the next row.

source.pages: not read; figure taken from a summary in a search result

income_by_occupation.stated: From a peak of slightly over 200 days (about 1325) the days a day labourer needed to match an annual worker's income fell to just above 100 by about 1350 and stayed below 150 until about 1525.
income_by_occupation.read_via: search-result summary only (the article and the Snopes page that quotes it were not readable)
income_by_occupation.note: Weakest-evidence row in this section: second-hand. It bounds how many days of casual work a household could have found, if labourers took the better of day work or a year's contract. The working paper EHES 121 and Oxford discussion paper are the readable-at-source routes and were PDF-only.

No source read states a smallholder's (cottager's or half-virgater's) net produce in money for 1370-1400. Dyer, Standards of Living in the Later Middle Ages (1989), ch. 7 'Peasants' is the standard place; its text was paywalled (Cambridge Core returned the chapter summary only). Not estimated.

No source read gives annual household income for a landless labourer in 1370-1400. Day rates are sourced above, but the days worked are contested (260 as a convention against roughly 100 break-even days), so the product is not computed here. The keeper must choose and label it.

No source read counts days actually worked by building craftsmen in the 1370s-1390s. Rogers (1884, p. 328) records contract payment 'for every day in the year' to carpenters at Windsor in 1408, i.e. paid-days, not worked-days.

subsistence.value_basis: midpoint of the stated 6d-8d; the 8d reading is from a damaged OCR ('Sd.')
subsistence.unit: pence per week, one adult, food under contract

source.citation: Rogers, J. E. Thorold, Six Centuries of Work and Wages (1884), ch. XII 'Labour and Wages'

subsistence.stated: Maintenance under contract was about 6d. to 8d. a week; the full board price was about a shilling a week, often less; wages were 'twice or three times the cost of his maintenance under contract'.
subsistence.note: A contract price for artisans' board, not a peasant's own cost. 6d-8d a week is 312-416d a year per adult; this is Rogers's arithmetic base, not a figure computed from a basket.

No readable source gives the annual money cost of a basic diet and necessities for a household of a stated size in 1370-1400. Horrell's 'Household consumption and the consumer price index, England, 1260-1869' (Economic History Review, 2023) builds a basket for a labouring family of five but its values are in figures and tables that were not readable (Wiley returned 403; the EHS blog page gives text only). Allen (2001) and Dyer (1989) were paywalled. Not estimated.

No source read gives a rent in money for a cottage or a standard holding in 1370-1400. Rogers (1884, ch. II, p. 40) converts a thirteenth-century Cuxham serf's rents and services to money but the figure is garbled in the OCR and is not the period.

Rogers (1884, p. 330) opens a sentence 'From 1260 to 1400 inclusive, the price of wheat is' but the figure is garbled in the OCR. Munro's and Clark's price series were PDF-only. Rogers p. 274 says only that the price of corn in the last twenty years of the fourteenth century was 'greatly below the average'.

mortality.stated: DeWitte: an estimated 30-50 percent of the European population in 1347-51. Mullan: roughly one-third to one-half.
mortality.note: Context for the plague-year row; not a non-plague rate. The two sources agree.

source.citation: Mullan, J., Cardiff Historical Papers (2007); DeWitte, PLoS ONE 9(5) (2014) e96513, Discussion, citing Roehrkasten for London wills

mortality.stated: Mullan: 1361-2, 1369, 1379-83 and 1389-93, and at least 13 more in the following century. DeWitte: London wills show plague mortality spikes in 1361, 1368, 1375, 1382 and 1390.
mortality.note: The sources differ on 1368 vs 1369 and on whether the early 1370s epidemic is 1375; value is Mullan's list, DeWitte's in stated. Neither gives a death share for these years.

Mullan (2007) says the 1361-2 epidemic was sex-selective and tests it on entry fines of the bishop of Winchester's estate, but the abstract page read gives no rate; the PDF was not readable. A search snippet of 'a little over 9 percent' at Halesowen could not be traced to Razi's text and is not used.

mortality.unit: years of further life at age 20 or 25
mortality.note: Searched: Hatcher, Piper and Stone, 'Monastic mortality: Durham Priory, 1395-1529', Economic History Review 59 (2006), pp. 667-687 (login-only; abstract says monastic expectancy fell sharply in the second half of the fifteenth century and the link to general mortality 'remains difficult to determine'); Jonker, Mathematical Population Studies 16 (2009), pp. 131-152 (abstract only: Crown tenants, before and during the Black Death). A secondary Conversation piece (DeWitte, 2022) states 31.3 years at birth for landowners' sons and 25.7 more years at 25, but its first DOI resolves to an unrelated paper (Carrieri and Serraino 2005, popes and artists), so the attribution is unreliable and the figures are not used.
No source read gives infant or child mortality for a late-fourteenth-century English village. Not estimated.
